text:
Microsoft’s Recall feature became a privacy scandal in 2024 because it was initially designed as an opt-in "photographic memory" that took screenshots of the user's screen every few seconds, capturing sensitive content such as passwords and private messages by default [Source: ev-1]. Despite Microsoft claiming the data would be encrypted, security researchers demonstrated that these screenshots were stored unencrypted (in plaintext) within a local SQLite database, making them accessible to any process running under the user account [Source: ev-1]. This discrepancy between security claims and actual implementation, combined with the default-on nature of recording everything on-screen, triggered investigations from regulators including the Irish Data Protection Commission, the UK Information Commissioner’s Office, and the Washington State Attorney General [Source: ev-1].

In response to this controversy, which marked the first major privacy crisis in the AI PC era, Microsoft delayed the feature's release in June 2024 and fundamentally reversed its defaults [Source: ev-1]. The relaunched version is now opt-in (default OFF) rather than enabled by default [Source: ev-1]. Additionally, accessing the timeline now requires Windows Hello authentication and presence detection, while incognito mode and DRM content are explicitly excluded from capture [Source: ev-1]. This revised, more secure version of Recall reached general availability on Copilot+ PCs in 2025 [Source: ev-1].
